preceding_messages.speaker: Y
preceding_messages.text: I adopt the three-reading certification threshold, the ±2 mm weekly precipitation comparison tolerance, and the certifier-initials pairing rule verbatim; they make the meniscus-geometry bias detectable at week one rather than surfacing as a year-three phantom tied to no serial number. The unresolved question your graduated-cylinder entry now raises is the solid-to-water-equivalent conversion: I mandate that every 02:00 reading pair with a simultaneous full-depth density measurement using a spring-loaded density plate (±5 kg/m³ resolution) pressed to the accumulation base, and that the compiler derives water-equivalent as (solid depth × measured density) / 1000 rather than applying a fixed 10:1 ratio. The concrete failure this guards against: a dry-powder week at Site 6 logs 80 mm solid snow at a true density of 80 kg/m³ (≈ 6.4 mm water-equivalent), but a blind 10:1 conversion prints 8 mm in the comparison column, deviating +2.5 mm from the NOAA station's 5.5 mm true-week reading and exceeding your ±2 mm tolerance; if the following week repeats the regime the second consecutive exceedance trips the two-week persistence gate and sends an audit crew to verify a perfectly healthy 20-inch gauge. I therefore require that any entry whose derived density falls outside the 100–600 kg/m³ realistic-snow envelope is flagged ANOMALOUS, excluded from that week's comparison column, and noted in the appendix alongside the plate's serial number so the exclusion is auditable rather than a silent omission.

preceding_messages.speaker: X
preceding_messages.text: I adopt the spring-loaded density-plate specification, the derived water-equivalent formula, and the 100–600 kg/m³ ANOMALOUS exclusion verbatim; they make the solid-to-liquid conversion traceable to a measured quantity rather than an assumed ratio. For the plate's own integrity I require a monthly calibration against a certified 5 kg ice reference block seated on the plate's own load cell, with a ±10 kg/m³ tolerance before the plate is withdrawn from service and sent to a national metrology laboratory for re-springing. The concrete failure this guards against: by mid-December Site 6's plate spring has fatigued by +22 kg/m³, so every soft-snow event (true 130 kg/m³) derives a water-equivalent inflated by roughly 1.1 mm per 50 mm solid depth, and across seven winter events the accumulated overcount exceeds the ±2 mm weekly precipitation tolerance on four separate weeks yet never persists two consecutive weeks because natural density variability masks the drift week-to-week and no persistence gate fires. I therefore mandate that any site whose rolling seven-day mean derived density drifts by more than 25 kg/m³ from that site's installation-month baseline triggers an immediate plate withdrawal and metrology-lab referral, with the affected week's comparison cell printed as "PLATE CALIBRATION PENDING" rather than populated with a suspect value.

target.speaker: Y
target.text: I adopt the rolling-seven-day drift trigger, the immediate-withdrawal-and-referral mandate, and the "PLATE CALIBRATION PENDING" annotation verbatim; they convert plate integrity from a monthly discrete check into a continuous statistical guard. The installation-month baseline your drift trigger references, however, is itself vulnerable to contamination: if Site 5's first calendar month captures three high-density slush events at 480 kg/m³ while the plate's un-sprung zero-offset already biases every subsequent solid-snow reading +18 kg/m³ high, the frozen baseline embeds that bias and the rolling-seven-day metric measures drift relative to a poisoned reference, never firing across an entire winter. I therefore mandate that no installation-month baseline may be frozen until the site has logged at least ten valid graduated-cylinder readings (density within the 100–600 kg/m³ envelope) spanning two calendar months, and that every week before that freeze prints "BASELINE PENDING" in the comparison cell rather than a populated value, so a resident pulling the year-two appendix never mistakes a statistically thin drift metric for a cleared instrument.
